# Preface {.unnumbered}

I wrote my undergraduate thesis in Earth Engine as a Geophysics student at Universitas Padjadjaran, in the DRPRS lab. Geophysics taught me to measure what I cannot touch; years of environmental work taught me what is worth measuring. I did not know then that the same few lines of code would follow me for years: to a carbon start-up in Germany, to plantation forests in Riau, to research with partners in Singapore and forestry teams in Brazil, and finally back to a lecture hall at UNSW Sydney.

Each of those places taught me something the tutorials had not. A map can look clean and still be wrong, because the numbers in the image were never understood as physics. A model can score 94 per cent and still fail in the field, because the samples sat next to each other. A client does not want a classifier; they want to know where, how much, and how sure. This book is those lessons, written down in the order I wish I had learned them: first what a sensor actually measures, then the code, then the problems people pay to have solved.

Most of it comes from project work. Some of it comes from the classroom, where I finally had time to ask why the methods I had been using for years actually work. Both are here, side by side, and every chapter ends with something you can run yourself.

## Why this book is free

I had the privilege of learning this work on real projects, next to good people, with real problems to solve, and of studying it further at UNSW Sydney with an LPDP scholarship. Not everyone gets that chance. I want everyone in this field to be able to experience it too, and to have peers to work through the hard problems with. This book shares it: the hands-on knowledge I have gathered, written down and given away, so that a student in Kupang, a forestry officer in Riau, a young engineer anywhere, can build the same skills and grow from them.

It is not a degree, and it does not replace a bachelor's programme or any formal training; I have not yet finished my own Master's. It is one practitioner's experience, made open, so that anyone willing to work through it can become a GIS or remote sensing specialist.

The need is urgent. Indonesia is a vast tropical country, close to two million square kilometres of land with the world's fourth-largest population, and it is where climate change arrives early: heavier rain on steep, crowded hillsides, floods in cities that are also sinking, fire in drained peat in every strong dry season, and rising seas on low coasts where millions live. The answers are spatial. Policy needs maps to set targets and report against them; planners need them to decide where to build and where not to; enforcement needs them to find illegal clearing, mining and fishing before the damage is done. That makes data precious, and for a country this size it cannot come from field surveys alone. It has to come from satellites and from platforms large enough to cover a whole district, or the whole country, every year. The data itself is now largely free. What is missing is people trained to turn it into decisions. That is why the book is free and open: every person who learns to do this well becomes a multiplier, mapping a district, training a team, and making the next decision better informed. This book is my contribution to that, and an invitation: learn it, use it, improve it, and solve the next problem together.

## Who this is for

**Environmental scientists, foresters and marine practitioners.** You know the ecosystem. You need the computation to stop being the bottleneck. No programming background is assumed; Chapter [-@sec-javascript] starts from what a variable is.

**GIS professionals moving from desktop to cloud.** Most of what you know transfers. The parts that do not, chiefly the server side execution model, are handled in Chapter [-@sec-server-side] before they can cost you a week.

**Developers and data scientists entering the geospatial domain.** Your coding is not the gap. Part I is where your reading should slow down, because a model trained on physically meaningless features will still report 94 percent accuracy.

**Students and trainers.** Every chapter ends with exercises, and the parts map onto teachable blocks. The [instructor notes](instructor.qmd) suggest course shapes for a five week bootcamp and a three day intensive.

: Reading pathways {.striped}

Three shortcuts through the material, depending on why you came.

**The minimum viable analyst.** Chapters [-@sec-physics], [-@sec-ecosystem], [-@sec-optical], [-@sec-cloud], [-@sec-sampling], [-@sec-supervised], [-@sec-accuracy]. From nothing to a validated land cover map with a defensible confusion matrix, in one weekend. This route is written in full.

**The GeoAI sceptic.** Chapters [-@sec-physics], [-@sec-sampling], [-@sec-supervised], [-@sec-embeddings]. Build a classifier the classical way, then rebuild it from satellite embeddings with a fiftieth of the training data, and judge the difference for yourself.

**The person with a deadline.** Chapter [-@sec-apps] first, then work backwards through whatever it depends on.

## How the code works

Every listing is a real file from `scripts/`, generated into the page at build time. Each chapter opens with two buttons: **Open in Code Editor** loads the JavaScript straight into Earth Engine, and **Open in Colab** opens the Python notebook, ready to run. Nothing here is pseudocode and nothing is a fragment that only works in context.

Under each listing is the output that code produced when the book was built: the real maps, charts and tables, not screenshots and not illustrations. That is deliberate. You can check your own run against it, a result is never described that the code did not actually produce, and when a number in the text looks surprising you can see where it came from. Where a chapter needs data that is not in Earth Engine or in a stable public archive, such as a drone image or a frozen timetable, the script downloads the exact files used for the book, so your run can match the printed one. Those [data snapshots](https://github.com/rifkynhsp-byte/Fullstack-Remote-Sensing/releases/tag/data-v1) are listed with their sources and licences.

The comments inside those scripts are the teaching, not decoration. Where a line encodes a decision that could reasonably have gone another way, the comment says which alternatives exist and why this one won. Reading a script top to bottom should feel like sitting beside someone narrating their reasoning.

::: {.callout-tip}

## How accurate are the maps in this book?

Every number in this book was produced by the code printed next to it, on public data, on the date the page was built. That makes every result checkable. It does not make every result decision-grade, and it is worth being precise about the difference.

**What an accuracy figure here means.** Most accuracies in the book measure agreement with a reference map (ESA WorldCover, Dynamic World, Global Mangrove Watch, a published inventory), not agreement with the ground. Where a chapter uses a global map as stand-in labels, it says so, and the number it reports is how well two maps agree. Only chapters with field plots, felled trees, gauge records or official statistics compare against measurements, and they name the source.

**Where the numbers move.** Rerunning a chapter months later can give slightly different figures: Dynamic World, GEDI and the embeddings are reprocessed, new scenes arrive, and random seeds are fixed but the data under them are not. Differences of a few per cent are expected; a different conclusion is not, and is worth reporting.

**Where the methods are weakest in Indonesia.** Closed canopy hides stems and blurs crowns; persistent cloud thins the optical record; smallholder mosaics are smaller than a 10 m pixel; global products are trained mostly elsewhere. The chapters show these failures rather than hiding them.

**What the maps are, and are not.** They are working demonstrations of methods, built to be audited. They are not certified products for land titles, carbon credits, legal enforcement, insurance pricing or engineering design. For those, they are the starting point.

**What it takes to make them decision-grade.** The path is well known, and each step is in the book:

1. **Local reference data, sampled properly.** A stratified random sample of field or high-resolution reference points, and area estimates with confidence intervals (Chapter [-@sec-accuracy]). This single step does more than any model change.
2. **Validation that cannot flatter.** Spatially blocked cross-validation and an independent test area (Chapter [-@sec-sampling]); report the error you would get in a new place, not the error next door.
3. **The right sensor for the object.** Drone imagery or LiDAR for single trees and small fields, radar where cloud never clears, field plots for biomass (Parts XV and VIII).
4. **Calibration against measurements.** Mill records for yield, gauges for floods, scaled logs for volume, census tables for people: every model in the book improves when one local measurement is added.
5. **Uncertainty in the deliverable.** A range, a probability or a confidence class next to every number, and the assumptions stated where a decision-maker will read them.

Found a number that looks wrong? Use **Ask a question** on that page. A reported error is a contribution, and the correction will be dated in the chapter.

## Conventions

::: {.callout-note}
## Concept
Background that explains why something works. Skippable on a first pass, worth returning to.
:::

::: {.callout-warning}
## Common failure
A mistake that is easy to make and hard to diagnose. Worth reading even if you skip everything else on the page.
:::

::: {.callout-important}
## Scientific integrity
A point where technically valid code still produces a scientifically indefensible map.
:::

::: {.callout-tip}
## From the field
Something that only shows up in operational work, usually the hard way.
:::

::: {.callout-tip appearance="simple" icon="false"}
**Run this chapter**
The box under every chapter title: open the chapter's code in the Earth Engine Code Editor or in Colab, in one click.
:::

## About the author

![](images/author.jpg){.author-photo width="170" fig-alt="Rifky Nauval Hendrawan"}

I'm **Rifky Nauval Hendrawan**, a remote sensing specialist from Indonesia, now living in Sydney. I use satellites, drones and data to help people understand and look after forests, land and the communities that depend on them.

My work has taken me from plantation forests in Riau to carbon projects with a climate start-up in Germany, research with partners in Singapore and forestry teams in Brazil. Today I am a Senior Remote Sensing Specialist at APRIL, and I am finishing a Master of Engineering Science at UNSW Sydney (December 2026).

I wrote this book because the most useful lessons in this field are learned on real projects, often the hard way, and they deserve to be shared freely, in English and in Bahasa Indonesia.

## Work with me

This book is free, and it will stay free. If it has been useful and you need the same methods applied to your own problem, I am open to:

- **Consulting and projects**: satellite and LiDAR analysis, forest inventory and biomass, carbon MRV, land-cover and change mapping, and Earth Engine applications, for companies, NGOs and government.
- **Training**: workshops and courses for teams, in English or Bahasa Indonesia, built on the chapters of this book.
- **Research collaboration and PhD opportunities** in remote sensing, LiDAR, GeoAI and environmental monitoring.

Write to [rifky.nhsp@gmail.com](mailto:rifky.nhsp@gmail.com) or [rifkynauvalhsp@gmail.com](mailto:rifkynauvalhsp@gmail.com), or connect on [LinkedIn](https://www.linkedin.com/in/rifkynauvalhsp). Corrections, disagreements and questions about the book are just as welcome. If you find an error, saying so is a contribution.
